title: Who failed, and when? The tool against someone else's labels
dek: Who&When holds {runs} failed runs of real agent teams, each with a human label of the agent and the step that caused the failure. The tool finds who talks to whom. It does not find who failed.
kicker: Who&When, a public dataset of failed agent runs

source.title: Which Agent Causes Task Failures and When? On Automated Failure Attribution of LLM Multi-Agent Systems
source.attribution: Excerpts are from Who&When: Zhang et al., "Which Agent Causes Task Failures and When? On Automated Failure Attribution of LLM Multi-Agent Systems", ICML 2025, arXiv:2505.00212; data at github.com/ag2ai/Agents_Failure_Attribution, MIT License, Copyright (c) 2025 Ming Yin. Each excerpt is cut short; nothing else is changed.
source.input: the Hand-Crafted runs, as logged (python3 -I agenttrace/failure_eval.py story who-failed-and-when)

runs.label: failed runs, each loaded as its own trace

undated.label: logged messages the tool holds as undated, and leaves out of its graph

logged.label: messages whose recipient the log names

kept.label: of them listed as a direct message, recipients kept

pair_found.label: logged sender-recipient pairs the tool finds, recipients withheld

pair_logged.label: logged sender-recipient pairs (one per pair per run)

msg_found.label: single addressed messages the tool finds, recipients withheld

sign_agent.label: runs where the record of the tool's first sign is by the labelled agent

sign_step.label: runs where it is the labelled step

chance_agent.label: chance for the agent (mean of one over the agents in a run)

busy_agent.label: runs where the agent with most records is the labelled agent

last_agent.label: runs where the last speaker is the labelled agent

published_agent.label: the dataset paper's best method, agent level (not re-measured)

alert.label: runs where the Alert rule fired (step clock)

watch.label: runs where the Watch rule fired (step clock)

label_ok.label: runs where the labelled step was spoken by the labelled agent

body.h: A dataset with the answer written down

body.p: Every accuracy number for this tool used to come from our own simulator. Who&When is someone else's data: [[c1|{runs} failed runs of real agent teams]], and for each one a person wrote down which agent made the decisive mistake and at which step. Nobody on this project made those labels.

The runs are not attacks and they are not swarms. Each is one small team working on one task. [[c2|No message carries a time]], only its place in the order. Loaded as logged, the tool cannot run its replay, and it leaves every logged message out of its graph.

In the hand-crafted runs the log names the recipient of each instruction. [[c3|{logged} messages are addressed this way]]. With the recipients kept, the tool lists all of them as direct messages once the records have a clock. That checks our reader. It is not an accuracy.

Then we took the recipients away. The tool saw who spoke, in what order, and the text. [[c4|It still found {pair_found} of the {pair_logged} sender-recipient pairs]]. It found far fewer of the single messages: [[c5|{msg_found} of {logged}]]. It counts each write once per reader, so it learns that the orchestrator talks to the web surfer, and not which instruction was which.

The tool has no feature that names a culprit. We read its flags as blame by rules fixed before any score was computed. [[c6|The record of its first warning sign is by the labelled agent in {sign_agent} of {runs} runs]], and chance is {chance_agent}. [[c7|Naming the agent with the most records does better: {busy_agent}]]. The dataset's authors report {published_agent} for their best method, a language model that reads the whole log.

One run shows why. [[c8|The annotators marked a click by the web surfer that landed on an unrelated page]]. The tool's first sign in that run is the orchestrator's opening plan, because that is where a second speaker first appears. A tool that looks for shared places, carried tokens and harmful actions has no reason to look at a wrong click.

Every run here is benign in the tool's sense: nothing is hidden and nobody is attacked. [[c9|On an order-only clock the Alert rule fired in {alert} of {runs} runs]]. It fires when a team talks. That is what it measures: information flow, not malice.

body.note: The steps of the hand-crafted runs come from Magentic-One, and the others from group chats built by an algorithm. Credit for the data and the labels is in the source line below and beside each excerpt.

docs.label: Who&When in the dataset registry: source, licence, what the tool can and cannot do with it

c1.caveat: Data and labels: Zhang et al., "Which Agent Causes Task Failures and When?", ICML 2025, arXiv:2505.00212, github.com/ag2ai/Agents_Failure_Attribution, MIT License, Copyright (c) 2025 Ming Yin. In a few runs the labelled step was not spoken by the labelled agent; both labels are scored as given.

c2.evidence: No record has a time, so nothing can be replayed as logged.
c2.caveat: Everything below that needs an order in time uses a step clock: each record is placed sixty seconds after the one before. It keeps the order and invents nothing else.

c3.evidence: An instruction whose recipient the log names.

records.note: The log's role for this record is "Orchestrator (-> WebSurfer)": sender and recipient are both written down.

c4.evidence: Pairs found with the recipients removed.
c4.caveat: A pair is a sender and a recipient inside one run. The tool also reports pairs the log does not address, such as an answer going back to the orchestrator; those are not shown to be wrong.

c5.evidence: Single messages found with the recipients removed.

records.note: The web surfer answers. With recipients withheld, the tool links it to the orchestrator because it posts next in the same conversation.

c6.evidence: The tool's first sign, read as blame.
c6.caveat: A run where the tool raises no sign counts as a miss. The interval and the per-subset figures are in reports/external/who_and_when/summary.md.

c7.evidence: Two baselines that use no tool, and the published result.
c7.caveat: The published figure is quoted from the paper's abstract for scale. We did not re-run it.

c8.evidence: The step the annotators marked in one run.

records.note: The labelled mistake. The label's reason: "WebSurfer clicks on an irrelevant website and disrupts the task-solving process."

c8.caveat: Excerpt and label from Who&When (Zhang et al., ICML 2025; MIT License, Copyright (c) 2025 Ming Yin).

c9.evidence: The default rules on benign runs.
c9.caveat: Counted once per run, on the step clock. A rate per day would mean nothing here and none is given.
